title: A denarius was a day's pay
summary: Jesus' own parable prices a day in the vineyard at one denarius, and a soldier under Tiberius earned less than that. It is the yardstick for every other sum in the Gospels.
body: In the parable of the vineyard the landowner agrees with the labourers 'for a denarius a day' (Matthew 20:2) and pays every worker exactly that: the parable takes a denarius as a day's pay for hired work in the fields.

Tacitus records mutinous legionaries in AD 14 complaining that 'ten asses a day is the value set on life and limb' — ten asses is five-eighths of a denarius, so a farm hand in the parable was paid better per day than a Roman soldier (though the soldier was paid year-round).

The coin itself was a small silver piece about 19 mm across, roughly the size of a modern US penny or a 1-euro-cent coin, weighing about 3.9 g of nearly pure silver. Matthew 22 says only that Jesus was handed a denarius bearing an 'image and inscription'. The denarius of Tiberius known as the 'tribute penny' carries his head and the legend TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS, 'Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus'.

title: A year's wages poured out in one act
summary: The onlookers price the flask of nard at 'more than three hundred denarii'. At a denarius a day that is roughly a year of a labourer's income, and Pliny gives prices for the costliest perfumes in the same range.
body: Mark and John both put a number on the perfume: over 300 denarii (Mark 14:5; John 12:5). John adds the quantity — a litra, the Roman pound of about 327 g — and the grade, 'pure nard'.

Set beside Matthew 20:2 (one denarius = one day's work), 300 denarii is about 300 working days. How many days a labourer actually worked in a year is an estimate: a six-day week minus Sabbaths and the pilgrim festivals leaves roughly 300, about a year's wages. The figure is a comparison, not a conversion into modern money.

Pliny the Elder, writing a generation later, lists prices for luxury unguents in this range: raw spikenard at 100 denarii per pound, and the costliest compounded perfume at 'from 35 to 300 denarii' per pound. He also notes that 'unguents keep best in alabaster boxes' — the very container Mark describes (see the Models tab for the flask).
Nard (Nardostachys jatamansi) grows in the Himalayas, so a pound in Judea had come by the Indian trade routes.

media.caption: Calcite ('alabaster') alabastron, Egypt, Ptolemaic period (305–31 BC). The long neck and narrow mouth kept perfume from evaporating; the neck was often snapped to open it, matching Mark's 'she broke the jar'.

title: Ten thousand talents: a debt bigger than the kingdom's tax income
summary: A talent was 6,000 denarii, so the first servant owed 60 million days' wages; Josephus says the whole of Herod's kingdom yielded about 900 talents a year. The second servant owed 100 denarii — about four months.
body: The parable sets the two debts side by side. A talent was not a coin but a weight of silver reckoned at 6,000 drachmae/denarii, so 10,000 talents is 60,000,000 denarii. At one denarius a day, that is 60 million days of labour — about 200,000 years for one worker (an estimate that assumes roughly 300 working days a year).

For scale, Josephus records the annual tax revenue of the territories Herod the Great left to his sons: 600 talents for Archelaus (Judea, Samaria, Idumea), 200 for Antipas (Galilee and Perea) and 100 for Philip — about 900 talents a year for the whole region. The servant's debt is more than eleven years of the entire kingdom's revenue. 'Ten thousand' (myrioi) was also the largest single number-word in Greek.
The fellow servant's 100 denarii is about four months' pay.

title: The widow's two lepta
summary: Mark translates her gift for Roman readers: two lepta 'make a quadrans' — 1/64 of a denarius, about eleven minutes of a labourer's twelve-hour day.
body: The lepton ('thin one') was the smallest bronze coin in circulation in Judea, the Jewish prutah. Most of those found in Jerusalem excavations were struck a century or more earlier under the Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus (103–76 BC) and were still in everyday use, worn and small.

Mark's aside, 'which make a kodrantēs' (Latin quadrans), fixes the value: a quadrans was a quarter of an as, and sixteen asses made a denarius, so her two coins were 1/64 of a day's wage. The arithmetic is exact; the 'eleven minutes' takes the twelve-hour working day the Gospels assume (John 11:9; Matthew 20:6-12).

title: The two-drachma tax and the coin in the fish
summary: Every adult Jewish male owed a half-shekel a year to the temple (Exodus 30:13). The Mishnah reckons the sanctuary shekel by Tyre's, and a Tyrian shekel, a stater of four drachmae, paid for exactly two men.
body: The collectors ask whether Jesus pays 'the two-drachma tax'. That is the annual half-shekel of Exodus 30:13, reinterpreted after the exile as a standing temple levy (Nehemiah 10:32 has a third of a shekel; by the first century it was a half). The Mishnah (Shekalim 1:3) describes money-changers setting up tables in the provinces a month before Passover to collect it.

The Mishnah reckons the sanctuary's shekel 'using a Tyrian maneh' (Bekhorot 8:7), and requires the yearly half-shekel to be given in coin. Tyre's shekels bore the image of the god Melqart. A Tyrian shekel was a tetradrachm — four drachmae — so the single stater Peter finds in the fish (Matthew 17:27) covers two half-shekel payments: 'for me and for you'.
See the Models tab for the coin's proportions.

title: Thirty pieces of silver
summary: Thirty shekels is the Torah's compensation for a slave killed by an ox. Matthew names no coin, so any modern value is an estimate — if they were Tyrian shekels it was about five months' wages.
body: Matthew is the only Gospel to give the price. He sets it beside a prophecy he credits to Jeremiah (27:9-10), whose words are close to Zechariah 11:12–13, where the prophet is paid 'thirty pieces of silver', 'this magnificent price at which they valued me', and throws it to the potter in the house of the LORD. Exodus 21:32 sets thirty shekels as what an owner receives for a slave gored to death.

The coin type is not stated. The Mishnah reckons Exodus's thirty shekels in the sanctuary shekel, 'using a Tyrian maneh' (Bekhorot 8:7). If the priests paid in that currency, Tyrian shekels (see the temple-tax card), thirty of them would be 120 denarii — about five months of a labourer's pay, at roughly 300 working days a year. That conversion is an inference, not a datum.

title: Two denarii at the inn
summary: The Samaritan leaves two days' wages with the innkeeper and promises to repay whatever more he spends.
body: Two denarii is two days of a labourer's pay (Matthew 20:2). How many nights that bought is an estimate. Polybius, in the second century BC, says innkeepers in the Po valley gave a guest 'enough of all they require for half an as per diem', a figure he gives to show how cheap that country was; at that rate two denarii (32 asses) would buy 64 days. Luke gives no price. The Samaritan adds, 'whatever more you spend, I will repay you'.

title: Twenty shekels for Joseph — and why the number keeps rising
summary: Joseph is sold for twenty shekels of silver, Exodus fixes the compensation for a gored slave at thirty, and Assyrian records of a few centuries later run to fifty or sixty. Kenneth Kitchen argues that each biblical figure sits near the going rate in the period its story is set in.
body: Genesis 37:28 prices Joseph at twenty shekels of silver. Exodus 21:32 sets thirty shekels as what an ox's owner pays when the animal gores someone else's slave. Leviticus 27:3-7 scales vow-valuations from three to fifty shekels by age and sex. Zechariah 11:12-13 has a shepherd paid off with thirty pieces of silver, 'this magnificent price at which they valued me'.

Kitchen, drawing on the cuneiform sale contracts Isaac Mendelsohn collected, gives a price curve. In the Third Dynasty of Ur, around 2100-2000 BC, ten shekels is the commonest price for a slave. Through the first half of the second millennium — roughly 1800-1700 BC, the Old Babylonian period — twenty shekels is the standard figure, and Hammurabi's laws assume it. Texts from Nuzi and Ugarit in the later second millennium sit around thirty. By about 1000 BC Assyrian documents are recording fifty to sixty shekels for a male slave, and Persian-period prices are higher still.

Kitchen argues that twenty, thirty and the Leviticus scale each land near the going rate for the era each text is set in, and that the traditions therefore preserve period detail rather than being composed wholesale at a much later date.
The contract prices are evidence; the inference from them to the age of the biblical traditions is Kitchen's argument, and this card is marked as an interpretation for that reason.

title: Why there were money changers in the temple at all
summary: The Mishnah reckons the sanctuary's shekel by Tyre's, and Tyre's shekels, of high silver, carried the head of a Phoenician god. The Gospels set money changers' tables in the temple courts.
body: Exodus 30:13-15 requires every man counted in Israel to give half a shekel 'according to the shekel of the sanctuary'. By the Second Temple period this was an annual levy, collected before Passover, and the Mishnah reckons the shekel of the sanctuary 'using a Tyrian maneh', and requires the half-shekel to be given in coin (Bekhorot 8:7).

From about 126 BC the mint of Tyre struck shekels and half-shekels of high silver, which assays put at roughly 94-97%, and held that standard for well over a century. The Mishnah does not give its reason for reckoning by Tyre's coin.

The Tyrian shekel carries the head of Melqart-Heracles on the obverse and an eagle on the reverse, with the legend 'of Tyre the holy and inviolable'. The coin by which the temple's dues were reckoned bore a Phoenician god.

In Mark, Jesus overturns the tables and says, 'Is it not written: My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations? But you have made it a den of robbers' (11:17, quoting Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11).
The same coinage stands behind Matthew 17:24-27, where the two-drachma tax for two men is settled with a single stater — a Tyrian shekel being worth four drachmas.

title: The lost coin, and why she lit a lamp to find it
summary: A drachma was about a day's wage, and the woman of the parable has ten. She lights a lamp and sweeps the house to find the one she lost.
body: The Greek drachma was roughly equivalent in value to the Roman denarius, and Jesus prices a day's labour at a denarius elsewhere (Matthew 20:2). Ten drachmas is therefore something like a fortnight's earnings for a labourer.

Kenneth Bailey describes the village house of the period as one room with a beaten-earth or rough stone floor and one small high window or none, dark in the corners even at midday. In the parable she lights a lamp, sweeps the house, and searches carefully until she finds it (15:8).

Bailey also reports the suggestion that the ten coins were a woman's marriage headdress or dowry ornament, strung as a set, and presents it as a possibility from later Near Eastern custom. Luke says nothing of it, and no first-century evidence for it in Galilee is cited.
